titulo.texto: Community Painting on Amate Paper from Xalitla, Guerrero

frase_gancho.texto: A people who tell the story of their lives in miniature, in ink, on bark paper.

puente_narrativo.texto: From paper we move on to the offering. Look for an altar of green corn: tender ears with their husks, arches of yellow flowers, and fresh corn tamales.

guion_corto.texto: This painting, made on amate paper, comes from Xalitla, a Nahua town on the Balsas River, in Guerrero. The painters use very fine brushes and black ink, and they fill the whole sheet with tiny figures: weddings, corn plantings, festivals, bullfights, dances, and fishing in the river. It is a chronicle of the town told in images, where every person and every animal has a place. The paper comes from San Pablito, in the mountains of Puebla, and the painters of Guerrero adopted it in the mid-twentieth century, when they moved to paper the fine drawing they had once used to decorate their clay vessels. There are no empty spaces: the image is made to be read little by little, like a book.

guion_largo.texto:
The paper of this painting comes from San Pablito, the Otomí town in the mountains of Puebla that you have already come to know, and the hands that painted it are Nahua, from the Balsas River basin, in Guerrero. It is the same basin where corn is thought to have been domesticated, about nine thousand years ago. In other words, this is a work made between two peoples with different languages, on a paper that travels from one mountain range to another.

The story is more recent than you might expect. In the mid-twentieth century, the potters of towns like Ameyaltepec and Xalitla decorated their pots with drawings of birds and flowers. When they tried amate paper, those drawings passed from clay to paper, and from a few birds they moved on to complete scenes of town life. It is one of the youngest folk arts you will see in the museum, but with very ancient roots.

Each painting is a chronicle. There is a wedding with music, a group planting corn, a fisherman in the river, a procession, a bullfight, and a little fireworks bull. There are also dances, like that of the tecuanes, in which the dancers put on jaguar masks and portray, according to tradition, the hunt for an animal that attacks the cattle. It is another of the dances with animal masks that the Toltec Hall told you about.

These painters have been called tlacuilos, a very old Nahuatl word: it was the name of the Mexica painters and scribes, the ones who made the codices. And the codices, as you already know, were painted on amate or on deer hide. In a way, these paintings are an inheritance of that craft: telling the life of a community with images, so that everyone can read it.

Come closer and notice the size of the details. The painters use extremely fine brushes, and each figure measures barely a few millimeters. Some work only with black ink on the natural brown of the paper, and others add colors. Both ways are valid, but the black ink has a particular elegance, almost like an engraving.

Notice that there are almost no empty spaces. The houses, the trees, the clouds, the animals, and the people fill the whole sheet. That abundance says something: that the life of a people is a sum of many things, and that all of them matter. A painting like this is not looked at all at once; it is read little by little, the way you read an illustrated book.

They are also an archive. If a hundred years from now someone wants to know how people dressed at a wedding in Guerrero, what a patron saint’s festival was like, or which animals lived in the river, they will be able to find out in a painting like this one. The painters, without meaning to, are leaving a record of their world.

And it is a work of coexistence. The paper made by the Otomí, the ink of the Nahua, the theme of the peoples of the Balsas: three things that come together on one sheet. If we had to choose one image for this museum, perhaps it would be this one: people who tell their story with what they have at hand.

texto.Technique/Material: Macerated amate bark, India ink and acrylic paint applied with a fine brush
texto.Function: Visual community chronicle, record of historical memory and contemporary Nahua art

texto.pregunta: Myth: Paintings on amate are as old as the codices.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Amate paper is extremely old, but this painting was born in the mid-twentieth century, when the painters of Guerrero moved from clay to paper.
